onThisDay.fits: 30 September 1882: the first hydroelectric power plant in the US began operating on the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin.
onThisDay.headline: A river lit a house for the first time
onThisDay.line: In Appleton, Wisconsin, a water wheel on the Fox River turned an Edison dynamo and lit two paper mills and a home.

funFact.fits: The first hydro plant, today in 1882.
funFact.statement: The first hydroelectric plant in America powered a whole town.
funFact.reveal: It lit two paper mills and the owner’s house, about twelve kilowatts. Hydro now makes about six percent of US electricity.

calmRead.fits: Expands today's On this day: the first hydroelectric plant, Appleton, 1882.
calmRead.title: The night the river turned on the lights
calmRead.teaser: Twenty-six days after Edison lit Manhattan, a paper-mill owner in Wisconsin did it with water.
paragraphs: H. J. Rogers owned a paper mill on the Fox River in Appleton, Wisconsin, and he had read about Thomas Edison. In the summer of 1882 he bought one of Edison's new dynamos, the kind meant to be turned by a steam engine, and did something Edison had not tried. He hooked it to the water wheel that already drove his mill.

On the evening of 30 September 1882 it worked. The dynamo lit the mill, a second mill down the river, and Rogers's own house, a big stone place called Hearthstone that still stands. About twelve kilowatts, enough for a few hundred of Edison's new bulbs. It was the first hydroelectric central station in the United States, and it came online just twenty-six days after Edison's coal-fired Pearl Street plant in New York.

The early months were comic. When the river ran fast the lights burned too bright and popped; when it ran slow they dimmed to orange. There was no regulator. Rogers's wife is said to have complained that the lamps in the parlor flickered whenever the mill upstream started a machine. But it was cheaper than steam, and it needed no coal.

Today about six percent of American electricity comes from falling water, and the great dams of the West, Hoover and Grand Coulee, are its grandchildren. They all descend from a paper mill, a water wheel and a man who read the newspaper.

word.meaning: Leaves, all of them together. In New England in October it is a season, an industry and a reason to sit in traffic on a country road.

kindness.text: Book the leaf drive now, with someone who has never seen a New England October. It goes fast.

joke.setup: Why did the first hydroelectric lights keep flickering?
joke.punchline: The river had not read the manual.
